cards.definition: The Catholic belief that God created the universe out of nothing, with no pre-existing matter.
The first book of the Bible, containing two accounts of Creation and the story of Adam and Eve.
Reading the Bible as factually and historically accurate in every detail, including the six-day creation account.
Reading the Bible as conveying religious truths through symbolism or metaphor, not as a scientific account.
The scientific theory, associated with Darwin, that species developed over millions of years through natural selection.
The belief held by many Catholics that God used the process of evolution as the means of creation.
The Catholic responsibility to care for and protect God's creation on His behalf.
The God-given authority over the natural world given to humans, as described in Genesis 1:28.
The belief that all human life is holy and sacred because it is created by God in His image.
Latin for 'image of God'; the Catholic belief that humans are uniquely created in the likeness of God.
The spiritual and immortal part of a human being, believed by Catholics to be given by God at conception.
The Catholic teaching that Adam and Eve disobeyed God in the Garden of Eden, introducing sin into the world.
The inherited tendency towards sin that Catholics believe all humans are born with as a result of the Fall.
The scientific theory that the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from a single point of infinite density.
An argument for God's existence based on the idea that everything has a cause, so the universe must have a first cause — God.
An argument for God's existence based on the apparent order and purpose in the universe, suggesting an intelligent designer.
Related to the idea that the universe has purpose or direction; used to describe arguments for God's existence from design.
All-powerful; a key attribute of God in Catholic theology, meaning God has unlimited power.
All-knowing; the Catholic belief that God has complete knowledge of everything, including past, present and future.
All-good and loving; the belief that God is perfectly good and acts out of love for humanity.
Evil and suffering caused by the free actions and choices of human beings, such as murder or war.
Evil and suffering caused by events in the natural world, such as earthquakes, disease, or floods.
The philosophical challenge of explaining how an omnipotent, omniscient and benevolent God can allow evil and suffering to exist.
An attempt to justify or defend God's goodness in the face of evil and suffering in the world.
The God-given ability for humans to make their own choices; Catholics believe this explains why God allows moral evil.
A supernatural force of evil in Catholic teaching, a fallen angel who tempts humans to sin.
The desire or enticement to do something wrong or sinful, which Catholics believe can come from the Devil.
The inner sense of right and wrong; Catholics believe it is the voice of God guiding moral decision-making.
The Catholic moral principle that right and wrong can be determined through reason and understanding of human nature, as taught by Aquinas.
The moral theory developed by Joseph Fletcher that the most loving action in any situation is always the right one.
The belief that certain actions are always right or wrong regardless of the circumstances or consequences.
The belief that whether an action is right or wrong depends on the context, culture or circumstances.
The laws given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai, forming the foundation of Catholic moral teaching.
Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5–7, including the Beatitudes, which outline how Catholics should live moral lives.
A series of blessings taught by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, describing the values of God's Kingdom.
Positive moral qualities or habits Catholics should develop; the cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance.
The teaching of Jesus to 'treat others as you would wish to be treated yourself' (Matthew 7:12).
The argument that God allows suffering because it helps humans develop morally and spiritually towards perfection.
The argument that God is not responsible for evil; evil entered the world through the free choices of humans and angels.
The official teaching authority of the Catholic Church, through which the Pope and bishops guide Catholics on moral issues.
An action, thought or omission that goes against God's will and damages the relationship between humans and God.
A very serious sin that completely destroys a person's relationship with God; it must be deliberate and freely chosen.
A less serious sin that weakens but does not destroy a person's relationship with God.
The Catholic sacrament in which a person confesses their sins to a priest and receives God's forgiveness and absolution.
The formal forgiveness of sins given by a priest during the Sacrament of Reconciliation.
Genuine sorrow for sins committed; Catholics believe true contrition is required before sins can be forgiven.
An act given by a priest after confession, such as prayers or good deeds, to show repentance and make amends.
The Catholic belief that Jesus' death on the cross freed humanity from sin and restored the relationship with God.
The reconciliation between God and humanity brought about by Jesus' sacrifice on the cross.
A parable told by Jesus (Luke 15) illustrating God's unconditional forgiveness and welcome for those who repent.
Jesus' parable in Luke 15 showing that God actively seeks out sinners and rejoices when they return to Him.
Turning away from sin and returning to God; Catholics believe repentance is necessary for forgiveness.
God's free and undeserved love and help given to humans, enabling them to live according to God's will.
The first sacrament in the Catholic Church, through which original sin is removed and a person becomes part of the Church.
The prayer taught by Jesus (Matthew 6:9–13) including the petition 'forgive us our trespasses as we forgive others'.
An approach to wrongdoing that focuses on repairing harm and restoring relationships rather than purely on punishment.
The use of the death penalty as punishment for a crime; the Catholic Church opposes capital punishment as incompatible with human dignity.
Physical punishment, such as caning; Catholics debate this in light of human dignity and the purpose of punishment.
The reasons for punishing wrongdoers: retribution, deterrence, reformation, protection and vindication.
Catholic Agency for Overseas Development; a Catholic organisation working for justice, peace and against poverty worldwide.
The Catholic belief that Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day, and that all humans will rise at the end of time.
Existence after physical death; Catholics believe in Heaven, Hell and Purgatory as possible destinations after death.
The state of eternal happiness and union with God, given to those who die in a state of grace.
The state of eternal separation from God, freely chosen by those who die in a state of mortal sin.
In Catholic teaching, a state of purification after death for those who are saved but not yet fully prepared for Heaven.
The Catholic belief that after death, all humans will be judged by God for their actions in life.
The Catholic belief that each soul is judged individually by God immediately after death.
The final judgement of all humanity at the end of time, when God will judge the living and the dead.
Deliberately ending a person's life to relieve suffering; the Catholic Church teaches this is always wrong.
Helping someone to take their own life, usually by providing the means; opposed by the Catholic Church.
Medical care focused on relieving pain and improving quality of life for those who are terminally ill, supported by the Catholic Church.
The deliberate termination of a pregnancy; the Catholic Church teaches that abortion is always gravely wrong.
The point at which Catholics believe God gives a soul to a developing human being; traditionally believed to be at conception.
Reports by some people of experiences during clinical death, sometimes used as evidence for life after death.
The belief that the soul survives death and continues to exist eternally, separate from the physical body.
The Second Coming of Christ at the end of time, when Catholics believe Jesus will return to judge the living and the dead.
A Catholic funeral Mass offered for the soul of a deceased person, asking God for mercy and eternal rest.
The Catholic principle that human life must be protected from conception to natural death.
A key New Testament passage in which St Paul teaches about the resurrection of the body and the hope of eternal life.
Jesus' statement 'I am the resurrection and the life', a key verse affirming Catholic belief in resurrection and eternal life.
The belief in one God; the foundation of Jewish faith, expressed in the Shema: 'Hear O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One.'
The central prayer of Judaism (Deuteronomy 6:4–9) affirming belief in one God, recited morning and evening.
The first five books of the Hebrew Bible (also called the Five Books of Moses), containing God's laws and teachings for Jewish life.
A sacred agreement between God and the Jewish people; key covenants include those with Abraham and Moses.
The 613 commandments given by God in the Torah that Jewish people are obligated to follow.
A summary of core Jewish beliefs written by Maimonides, including belief in God's oneness, the Torah, and the coming of the Messiah.
In Judaism, the expected future leader anointed by God who will bring peace and redemption to Israel and the world.
A central text of Rabbinic Judaism consisting of the Mishnah and Gemara, containing Jewish law, ethics and debate.
A branch of Judaism that strictly adheres to traditional Jewish law and practice as divinely commanded.
A branch of Judaism that reinterprets traditional practices in light of modern life, emphasising ethical principles.
The Jewish principle that preserving human life overrides almost all other religious commandments.
Charity and justice in Judaism; giving to those in need is considered a religious obligation, not merely a kind act.
A Hebrew phrase meaning 'repairing the world'; the Jewish responsibility to act for justice and improve society.
The first patriarch of Judaism, with whom God made the covenant of circumcision, promising him many descendants and the land of Canaan.
The most important prophet in Judaism, who led the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Torah from God on Mount Sinai.
The Jewish account of God freeing the Israelites from slavery in Egypt under Moses' leadership, a foundational event in Jewish identity.
In early Hebrew thought, the shadowy underworld where all the dead exist; later Jewish belief developed ideas of resurrection.
Hebrew for 'the World to Come'; the Jewish belief in a future age of peace, or the afterlife and resurrection of the dead.
The Jewish belief that humans are given the freedom to choose between good and evil, and are therefore responsible for their actions.
Jewish concepts for the good inclination and evil inclination that exist within every person, between which humans must choose.
The Jewish day of rest observed from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, marked by synagogue worship, family and rest from work.
The Jewish place of worship, study and community gathering; the central institution of Jewish communal life.
A Jewish religious teacher and leader of the community, responsible for interpreting Jewish law and providing spiritual guidance.
The Jewish dietary laws that determine which foods are permissible (kosher) and how they must be prepared.
Food that meets the requirements of Jewish dietary law; for example, meat and dairy must not be eaten together.
The coming-of-age ceremony for Jewish boys (13) and girls (12/13), marking their responsibility for following Jewish law.
The Jewish practice of circumcising male babies on the 8th day after birth as a sign of the covenant with Abraham.
The Jewish New Year, a time of reflection and repentance, marked by the blowing of the shofar (ram's horn).
The Day of Atonement; the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, involving fasting, prayer and asking forgiveness from God.
A major Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt, celebrated with the Seder meal and retelling of the story.
The ritual meal held on Passover in which the story of the Exodus is retold using symbolic foods and the Haggadah.
The text read during the Passover Seder, telling the story of the Exodus from Egypt.
The Jewish festival of Tabernacles commemorating the 40 years the Israelites spent in the desert, celebrated in temporary shelters.
The Jewish festival of lights celebrating the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem and the miracle of the oil.
A small case containing a scroll with verses from the Torah (Shema), attached to doorposts of Jewish homes as a sign of faith.
Small black leather boxes containing Torah passages, worn by observant Jewish men during morning weekday prayers.
A Jewish prayer shawl with fringes (tzitzit) worn during morning prayers as a reminder of the commandments.
A small head covering worn by Jewish men as a sign of respect before God.
The practical application of preserving life in Jewish law; e.g. Shabbat rules may be broken to save a life.
Jewish tradition requires prompt and simple burial, with the body treated with respect; cremation is traditionally opposed.
